novelty.justification: The core method explicitly 'keeps the well-validated preference/bandit update loop of PDCAT' and mainly replaces its normalized reward and static constraints, so the paradigm is unchanged. This is a meaningful extension over prior flag-selection work such as R16's learned flag interactions and R35/R38's ML/BO-driven selection, but not a new mechanism or architecture.
novelty.rubric: Incremental: a meaningful extension or optimization of prior baseline work that fixes a concrete prior limitation, but the core paradigm is unchanged.
novelty.differentiation: Unlike R16's evolutionary flag-interaction learning, R35's static critical-flag selection, or R38's Bayesian optimization, ECCAT adapts reward normalization and interaction constraints online from the target program's own tuning history under a fixed budget.

feasibility.justification: The plan requires a unified harness, baseline drivers, and a full cBench/PolyBench grid across 58 programs and three budgets, with the context noting it 'may require several days of compute time.' This is nontrivial but standard research engineering; benchmarks and PDCAT code are available, and the artifact reports pilot completion.
feasibility.rubric: Moderate workload (sweet spot): needs nontrivial coding such as scripting existing open-source tools (parsers, CFG extractors) or building a custom graph-processing pipeline; standard research engineering effort.

clarity.justification: The What/Why/How are present: replace PDCAT's 'ad-hoc normalized reward' with an 'empirically anchored cumulative-margin preference reward' and learn 'pair-wise flag interactions.' However, exact reward formulas, interaction-mining algorithms, and detailed controls are deferred to referenced files and not specified in the artifact.
clarity.rubric: Complete frame but missing details: What/Why/How are present, yet key technical execution details or specific comparison plans are underspecified.

notes: Scores the intermediate idea artifact (not the final paper).
Dimensions: novelty, feasibility, clarity (each 1-5). Excitement removed.
Novelty is scored against a Solution Space built from mineru REFERENCES titles (+ related_work.json abstracts when matched).
idea_generation.summary: ECCAT extends PDCAT by replacing its fragile normalized reward with an empirically anchored cumulative-margin preference reward and learning pairwise flag interactions from tuning history. It targets a concrete reproducibility weakness and proposes a unified evaluation harness. However, the core paradigm remains PDCAT's preference bandit, technical details are underspecified, and the full benchmark evaluation is compute-intensive.
strengths: Identifies a concrete failure mode in PDCAT: permax/permin sensitivity and clipped normalized reward.
Proposes budget-adaptive empirical reward anchoring instead of fixed user-supplied bounds.
Includes a unified reproducible harness across five baselines and real benchmarks.
weaknesses: Core method inherits PDCAT's preference/bandit loop, limiting novelty.
No concrete formula is given for the cumulative-margin reward or pairwise interaction discovery.
Full experiment is compute-heavy and depends on authored baseline drivers.

claims.statement: PDCAT improves acceleration performance over GCC default -O3 optimization setting on all selected cases at 5,000 seconds.
claims.evidence_quote: PDCAT achieves 5.5%-81.2% acceleration performance over GCC default -O3 optimization setting in all 28 selected cases in 5,000 seconds.

claims.statement: PDCAT significantly outperforms four compared compiler auto-tuning techniques, including the state-of-the-art technique SRTuner.
claims.evidence_quote: PDCAT significantly outperforms the four compared techniques, including the state-of-art technique SRTuner.

claims.statement: PDCAT achieves the best optimization result on 10/11/14 programs at 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieve best results on only 2/1/1, 5/3/2, 3/5/4 and 8/8/7 programs, respectively.
claims.evidence_quote: PDCAT achieves the best optimization result on 10/11/14 programs in 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while the compared RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieve the best results on only 2/1/1, 5/3/2, 3/5/4 and 8/8/7, respectively.

claims.statement: PDCAT never achieves the worst result on 28 programs at 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, whereas baselines achieve worst results in multiple cases.
claims.evidence_quote: PDCAT never achieves the worst results on 28 programs in 1,250/2,500/5,000 seconds, while the compared RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner and SRTuner achieve the worst results in 18/18/21, 3/3/3, 6/5/3 and 1/2/1, respectively.

claims.statement: ECCAT replaces PDCAT's hand-set performance-bound reward with an empirically anchored running z-score of observed speedups.
claims.evidence_quote: The reward is the running z-score E_t = (s_t - mu_t)/sigma_t of observed speedups, which is scale- and shift-invariant, needs no user hyper-parameters, and adapts as the search progresses.

claims.statement: ECCAT mines pairwise flag interactions online from tuning history to bias sampling toward synergistic flags and away from conflicts.
claims.evidence_quote: Every 40 iterations, pairwise co-occurrence lift among the top-half-speedup histories is computed; positive lift biases collaborative sampling to co-enable synergistic flags, negative lift biases it to disable one of a conflicting pair.

claims.statement: ECCAT is more sample-efficient than PDCAT and RIO at 60-second budgets.
claims.evidence_quote: On 13 programs from cBench and PolyBench under a unified wall-clock protocol, ECCAT is more sample-efficient than PDCAT and RIO at short and medium budgets (median speedup ratio over -O3 of 1.16 vs. 1.10/---1.08 at 60 s).

claims.statement: The empirical reward anchor is the dominant contributor to ECCAT's performance based on ablations.
claims.evidence_quote: ablations show the empirical anchor is the dominant contributor.

claims.statement: PDCAT's reward normalization relies on user-supplied performance bounds that can distort preference signal when misspecified.
claims.evidence_quote: PDCAT normalizes by (speedup - p_min)/(p_max - p_min), where p_min, p_max are user-supplied performance bounds. Speedups outside [p_min,p_max] are clipped, and p_min=0.8 is unattainable ... so the preference signal is systematically distorted unless the user tunes these bounds per program.

claims.statement: Evaluation uses a shared wall-clock protocol and a unified evaluator for ECCAT and baseline methods.
claims.evidence_quote: We evaluate ECCAT against PDCAT, RIO, CFSCA, CompTuner, and SRTuner with a single shared evaluator and identical wall-clock accounting.
